subject: MGMT160
title: Management in Practice: Advice, Evidence and Your Development Plan

questions.stem: Identify the most repeated lesson of the course, according to advice 1.
options: Diagnose before you act — the visible problem is usually the symptom
Work harder than everyone else around you, because effort is what managers notice first
Get a title as early as possible, because people listen to the title before the person
Never admit a mistake in front of the team, because it weakens the manager's authority
questions.why: Ask 'why?' before 'what do we do?' — Chapters 4 and 7 compressed to a habit. See §10.1.

questions.stem: Explain advice 2, 'write goals with numbers and dates'.
options: 'Do better' is a mood; 'from X to Y by a date' is a goal
Goals should be long and detailed so that every possible situation is covered in advance
Only top managers need goals, because they are the ones who set the direction
Dates make goals impossible, because nobody can predict what will happen by then
questions.why: People who set measurable goals quietly outperform people who set wishes. See §10.1.

questions.stem: Describe advice 4, 'praise specifically, correct privately'.
options: Recognition in public, by name, for a real thing; correction one-to-one, about the work, never the person
Praise everyone equally so that nobody feels left out; correct in front of the team so that everyone learns
Never praise, because people become complacent; always correct, because that is how standards are kept
Praise privately so that colleagues are not jealous; correct publicly so that the lesson reaches everyone
questions.why: This single habit builds teams. See §10.1.

questions.stem: Explain why the four questions are cheapest to apply on small choices.
options: Big unethical decisions always start as small ones
Small choices do not matter, so the questions can be answered quickly without much thought
Large companies have lawyers for the big choices, so managers only need to handle the small ones
The four questions only work for small choices, because big decisions are too complex for them
questions.why: Protect your integrity early. See advice 5 in §10.1.

questions.stem: Explain advice 6, 'volunteer to lead small things'.
options: Leadership is a muscle; small reps now beat big titles later
Small tasks are the only ones students are allowed to do before they graduate
Leading small things earns a title quickly, because managers notice who volunteers
Big things should be avoided forever, because the risk of failing in public is too high
questions.why: The group project, the club event, the errand nobody wants to organise. See §10.2.

questions.stem: Explain why 'master the boring basics' matters.
options: Reliability is so rare that it reads as talent
The basics are the only thing managers do, so there is nothing else to master
Boring tasks pay the most, because nobody else is willing to do them
It makes the manager look busy, which protects them when results are poor
questions.why: Reply on time, arrive prepared, do what you said by when you said. See §10.2.

questions.stem: Identify the pattern across all ten pieces of advice.
options: None needs a title, a budget or an MBA — each is a behaviour you can start this week
All of them require a management degree, because they rest on theory students have not yet learned
All of them require a large budget, because recognition, training and tools cost money
All of them apply only after promotion, because a student has nobody to lead
questions.why: Exactly what Chapter 1 promised on its first slide. See §10.2.

questions.stem: Describe the strong move in the 'first leadership moment' — five members, no leader, nothing done.
options: Lead without announcing it: propose a simple plan with tasks, owners and dates, ask each person which piece they want, set one weekly check
Wait for someone to be appointed leader by the professor, because a group that chooses its own leader will argue about the choice
Complain to the professor that the group is not working and ask to be moved to a group that has a leader
Do all the work alone and put everyone's name on it, because that is faster than organising four other people
questions.why: Influence is leadership; the title is paperwork. Chapters 4, 5 and 7 on the same afternoon. See §10.3.

questions.stem: Describe the 'lollipop moment' from Drew Dudley's talk.
options: Leadership as the small moments that change someone's direction, often without knowing it
A reward given to the best employee at the end of each month in front of the team
A monthly team party at which the manager thanks everyone for their work
The moment a manager receives a title and realises that people now listen
questions.why: Watch Dudley first — it is the chapter's spirit. See §10.5.

questions.stem: Identify what drives people in thinking work, according to Dan Pink.
options: Autonomy, mastery and purpose
Bigger bonuses tied to measurable output
Strict supervision and clear instructions
Fear of losing the job to a competitor
questions.why: For thinking work, bigger rewards often worsen performance. See §10.5 and §10.6.

questions.stem: Identify the three one-minute tools in The One Minute Manager.
options: One-minute goals, one-minute praisings, one-minute redirects
One-minute meetings, one-minute emails, one-minute breaks
One-minute hiring, one-minute firing, one-minute promoting
One-minute plans, one-minute budgets, one-minute reports
questions.why: Agree what good looks like before work starts; catch people doing something right; correct promptly about the behaviour. See §10.6.

questions.stem: Describe Edmondson's finding on psychological safety.
options: Teams where members feel safe to speak up learn faster; teams reporting MORE errors were sometimes the better ones
Teams with no reported errors are always the best, because they have the most careful members
Safety means never disagreeing with the manager, so that the team stays united
Reporting errors should be punished, because teams that report many errors are making many errors
questions.why: They reported instead of hiding — which changes how a manager should react to bad news. See §10.6.

questions.stem: Identify the three things no dataset contains, according to the six studies.
options: Judgement under uncertainty, the ability to create safety for other people, and the habit of checking
Speed, memory and the ability to process large volumes of information
Typing, filing and scheduling the work of a team
Forecasting, summarising and drafting documents
questions.why: This is what to build during university. See §10.7.

questions.stem: Explain how the post-course scorecard should be used.
options: Rate yourself on evidence; your two lowest rows are the input for your plan, not failures
Rate yourself as high as possible, because confidence is the first quality of a manager
Compare your score with your classmates to see where you stand in the group
Ignore the low rows and build your plan around the skills you already have
questions.why: Scoring honestly matters more than scoring high. See §10.8.

questions.stem: Identify the four course tools a development plan uses to manage yourself.
options: Goals (Ch 4), resources (Ch 5), motivation by mastery (Ch 6), a checkpoint (Ch 7)
Salary, title, office and car
Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats
Fear, uncertainty, comfort and loss
questions.why: You are your own first employee. See the Part 1 summary and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Determine the strong response when a friend asks you to hide a mistake that cost money.
options: 'I won't report you behind your back — but this needs to be told, and I'll stand next to you while you tell it'
Stay quiet — nobody will know, and a friend who trusts you deserves loyalty more than the company does
Report the friend secretly to the manager, so that the problem is fixed without damaging the friendship
Fix the mistake yourself and say nothing, so that the money is recovered and nobody has to be told
questions.why: Hiding it fails fair, who is harmed, and the public test. Mistakes are forgivable; cover-ups end careers in slow motion. See §10.3.

questions.stem: Determine the professional move when a senior person dismisses your idea in one sentence.
options: Afterwards, privately: 'could I take five minutes to show you the numbers behind that idea?' — evidence, not feelings
Argue strongly in the meeting, because an idea that is not defended at once will never be taken seriously
Sulk and stop contributing, so that the senior person realises what the team is losing
Send the idea to the senior person's boss, who may be more open to new thinking
questions.why: People who handle 'no' well get more 'yes' later; evidence decides, not volume. See §10.4.

questions.stem: Determine the right response when your university suddenly changes a major system and the group chat is on fire.
options: Get the why first, give the new system an honest two weeks, and channel real problems into specific feedback through the right channel
Join the anger in the group chat, because the university needs to hear how strongly students feel about the change
Refuse to use the new system until the university explains the reasons for the change to every student
Transfer to another university whose systems are stable, because this one does not respect its students
questions.why: This is Chapter 8 happening to you; the calm, constructive voice during change is the fastest way to be noticed. See §10.4.

questions.stem: Analyse the four judgement scenarios. Determine the common thread.
options: Diagnose before reacting, bring evidence, protect both the relationship and the standard
Always obey the senior person, because experience is worth more than a new idea
Always report problems to the top, because that is where decisions are made
Avoid conflict at any cost, because a disagreement damages the relationship permanently
questions.why: That person is described in every chapter of the course. See §10.4.

questions.stem: Analyse a manager students remember badly. Determine the advice the chapter says such managers most often failed.
options: Advice 1, 3 or 4 — diagnose before acting, listen, praise specifically and correct privately
Advice 9 — use AI like a careful professional for routine work
Advice 10 — stay a student and keep learning after the course ends
Advice 6 — volunteer to lead small things before being given a title
questions.why: And the one remembered well did advice 4 without ever reading a management book. See §10.1.

questions.stem: Select the course company that failed Roselinde Torres's third question — 'are you courageous enough to abandon what made you successful?'.
options: Nokia
Careem
Kodak
Amazon
questions.why: Nokia perfected yesterday's phone — the success trap. See §10.5 and Chapter 8.

questions.stem: Analyse Dan Pink's claim that bigger rewards can worsen thinking work. Determine which course theories it supports.
options: Maslow's top layers, Herzberg's motivators and Theory Y
Taylor's pay-by-output and the one best way
Weber's bureaucracy and clear rules applied equally
Theory X and close supervision of every task
questions.why: Autonomy, mastery and purpose rebuild Chapter 6 from evidence. See §10.6.

questions.stem: Analyse the Gallup finding that the manager explains about 70% of engagement. Determine the question it raises for organisations.
options: Why do they still promote the best worker instead of the best people-developer?
Why do managers earn about 70% more than the members of their teams?
Why are about 70% of managers unhappy in their jobs?
Why do about 70% of employees want to become managers?
questions.why: See the discussion question in §10.6.

questions.stem: Determine how a manager should react to bad news, based on Edmondson's psychological-safety research.
options: Make it safe to report — teams that report errors learn faster than teams that hide them
Punish the person who reported it, so that the team takes more care in future
Ignore it to keep morale high, since the team is already under pressure
Report fewer errors upward so that the team looks better to senior managers
questions.why: Safety beats silence. See §10.6.

questions.stem: Analyse Tversky and Kahneman's finding that bias is built into all minds. Determine the implication for hiring.
options: Design systems against bias — structured criteria and checks — rather than relying on 'be objective'
Hire only people with no bias, which can be tested for during the interview
Let the most senior person decide alone, since experience reduces bias
Avoid hiring altogether and promote from inside, where people are already known
questions.why: If bias is universal, organisations should design against it. See §10.7.

questions.stem: Analyse the finding that AI lifts the weakest writers most. Determine what a new graduate should do and the risk that comes with it.
options: Use AI to raise routine performance fast — and verify everything, because speed brings the lawyer's risk
Avoid AI so as not to depend on it, because the skills that matter are built without it
Copy AI output to save time, because new graduates are judged on speed before quality
Use AI only for personal tasks, where a mistake costs nobody anything
questions.why: AI raises the floor; the careful users thrive, not the fastest copiers. See §10.7 and advice 9.

questions.stem: Select the development-plan goal that passes the course's own standard.
options: 'Deliver three presentations this semester, each opening with a hook and ending with one clear ask, feedback collected after each, by December'
'Become a better communicator over the coming year by taking every opportunity to speak in class, in meetings and in front of groups'
'Try to speak more in class, especially when I have something to say, and stop worrying about what the other students think of me'
'Improve myself as a future manager by reading, watching talks and practising the skills the course has shown me I need'
questions.why: Number, date, how — practise what you teach yourself. See Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Determine the purpose of the checkpoint in a development plan.
options: A date to re-take the scorecard and compare — Chapter 7's control applied to yourself
A reward for finishing the plan, which keeps the student motivated to the end
A meeting with the professor to discuss the plan and get it approved
The date on which the plan is written and signed by the student
questions.why: A plan without a checkpoint is a wish. See §10.8 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Compare 'minutes not hours' in The One Minute Manager with Mintzberg's finding that half of managers' activities last under nine minutes. Determine the relationship.
options: They fit — fragmented days reward short, precise goals, praisings and redirects
They contradict — Mintzberg says managers need long, uninterrupted meetings to lead well
They are unrelated, because one is about time and the other about motivation
Mintzberg proves the book wrong, because nothing useful can be done in one minute
questions.why: The discussion question in §10.6: does it contradict Mintzberg's chaotic days, or explain them?

questions.stem: Analyse the 'first leadership moment' solution. Identify the three chapters used on the same afternoon.
options: Chapter 4 (plan with tasks, owners, dates), Chapter 5 (participation builds commitment), Chapter 7 (one weekly check)
Chapter 1 (what managers do), Chapter 2 (history of management), Chapter 3 (the environment)
Chapter 8 (change), Chapter 9 (AI at work), Chapter 10 (becoming a manager)
Chapter 2 (history), Chapter 6 (leading and motivating), Chapter 9 (AI at work)
questions.why: See the answer to question 2 in §10.3.
